title: How to thread a needle for cross-stitch
subtitle: Threading a tapestry needle with stripped strands without a needle threader
excerpt: Threading a tapestry needle for cross-stitch uses the loop method: fold the stripped strands over the needle, pinch the fold flat, slide the needle out, and push the pinched fold through the needle eye. The loop is narrow enough to pass through without a threader when the strands have been properly stripped.
sourceNotes: Standard cross-stitch threading method. The loop method is documented in all major counted cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: A blunt-tipped needle that slips between fabric threads instead of piercing them. Size 24 is the default for 14-count Aida; larger numbers are finer needles for higher-count fabrics.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count and threads them together.

content.text: The loop threading method works on a
without a needle threader. Fold the stripped

over the needle, pinch the fold flat so it is nearly invisible, slide the needle out, and press the pinched fold through the eye. The fold is thin enough to push through cleanly when the strands have been stripped beforehand.
Strip the strands you need. Lay them together without twisting and hold the group in one hand.
Fold the group of strands in half over the shank of the needle, close to the eye end. Hold the fold in your fingertips with the needle inside the loop.

Pinch the fold tightly between thumb and forefinger, squeezing it flat. Then slide the needle upward out of the loop. Keep the pinched fold compressed; it should be barely visible between your fingers.
Present the eye of the needle to the pinched fold and press the fold through the eye. Push rather than pull; the fold is firm when pinched. It should pass through cleanly with light pressure.
Pull the loop through until a short tail sits on one side of the needle and the longer working length on the other. The tail should be no longer than 3 cm to avoid tangling at the end of each stitch.

items.symptom: The fold won't pass through the needle eye
items.cause: Too many strands for the needle size, or the strands were not stripped and lie twisted rather than flat.
items.fix: Check that you are using the right needle size (size 24 for 14-count with two strands). Strip the strands properly before folding. If two strands won't thread a size 24, try a size 22, which has a slightly larger eye.

items.symptom: The thread slips out of the needle after threading
items.cause: The tail is too short on one side, so the loop pulls free when the needle moves.
items.fix: Leave at least 3 cm of tail on the short side. The loop must sit securely through the eye with some tail to grip.

content.text: The loop method is faster than using a needle threader once it is practised. Try it with one strand, then two. For the loop start method of beginning a thread in the fabric, a looped thread makes the starting technique even quicker.
